title: Greetings
blurb: Say hello, goodbye and thank you.

items.mnemonic: Identical to English “hello” — a straight borrowing, no trick needed.
sut (how) + mae (is/there is) → literally “how is (it)?” — that mae turns up everywhere meaning “is/there is”.
bore (morning) + da (good) → word for word, “morning good”.
prynhawn hides nawn (noon) inside it, so think “near-noon” + da (good) → “good (near-)noon”.
nos (night) + gwaith (occasion/turn, the same -waith in unwaith “once”) + dda (good) → “good night-time”.
nos (night) + da (good) → literally “good night”.
hwyl literally means “sail” (as on a boat), and by extension “spirit/fun” + fawr (big) → picture a big sail catching the wind as you head off — “big spirit” as a send-off.
No clean breakdown — try the sound-trick: “DEE-olch” a bit like “the oil change” — thank the mechanic before you leave.
da (good) + iawn (very/right — also used alone to mean “okay!”) + diolch (thanks) → “good very, thanks”.
os (if) + gwelwch (you see, from gweld “to see”) + yn dda (well) → literally “if you see (it) well” — asking someone to “see fit” is the Welsh way of saying please.
Sound-trick: “KROY-so” sounds like “crows, oh!” — picture crows cawing you a big welcome.
iechyd (health, from iach “healthy”) + da (good) → “good health” — exactly like raising a glass and saying cheers.

title: Numbers 1 to 10
blurb: Count to ten.

items.mnemonic: Sounds like “een” — picture a single bean: un = one.
Sounds like “die” — picture two duellists facing off: dau = two.
Identical to the English prefix “tri-” (triangle, tricycle): tri = three.
Picture a four-legged “pet” marching off to WAR — ped-WAR: pedwar = four.
Sounds exactly like English “pump” — picture five pumps of a bike tyre: pump = five.
Rhymes with “heck” — roll a six and shout “chwech, heck yes!”: chwech = six.
Sounds like “scythe” — a scythe’s long curved blade is shaped a bit like a 7: saith = seven.
Sounds very close to the English word itself: “ooith” ≈ “eight” — the easiest one here: wyth = eight.
Sounds exactly like English “now” — picture needing nine things right now: naw = nine.
Sounds like “deck” — picture ten cards dealt on a deck: deg = ten.

title: Family and friends
blurb: The people closest to you.

items.mnemonic: Identical to English “mum/mam” — no trick needed.
Swap the letters of “dad” around — t-a-d — and you have tad.
Sounds like “browed” — picture a brother with furrowed brows: brawd = brother.
Sounds close to “choir” — picture singing in a choir with your sister: chwaer = sister.
Sounds like “nine” — a grandmother who’s lived nine lifetimes of wisdom. (North Wales word; the south says mam-gu, literally “dear mam”.)
Sounds like “tide” — picture a grandfather watching the tide roll in. (North Wales word; the south says tad-cu, literally “dear tad”.)
Contains plant — the plural “children” — think of a child as a little plant still growing: plentyn = child.
Nearly identical to English “friend” — just drop the e: ffrind.
Sounds like “tay-lee” — picture your whole family sitting down for te (tea) together: teulu = family.
Ends in tref, the same word you’ll meet in pentref (village) — cartref is literally your own personal “home-town”.

title: Food and drink
blurb: Order a cup of tea and a slice of bara brith.

items.mnemonic: Sounds like “BA-ra” — picture a loaf going “baa” like a sheep made of bread: bara = bread.
Sounds like “cause” — cheese is always the cause of a good sandwich: caws = cheese.
Sounds like a lithe, light “laith” — picture a thin white stream pouring: llaeth = milk. (South Wales says llefrith instead.)
Identical to English “tea”.
Identical to English “coffee”, just spelled Welsh-style.
Sounds like “door” — picture opening a door onto a waterfall: dŵr = water (the River Dover takes its name from this very old Celtic water-word).
Sounds close to “oval” — and apples are oval-ish: afal = apple.
Sounds like “KOO-roo” — picture a kangaroo chugging a pint: cwrw = beer.
bara (bread) + brith (speckled/mottled) → literally “speckled bread” — picture a loaf speckled with dried fruit.
Sounds like “kowl” — a chunky Welsh stew, close in sound and sense to English “cawl/coleslaw” roots.

title: Days and time
blurb: Days of the week, plus today, tomorrow and yesterday.

items.mnemonic: dydd (day) + Llun (Moon, same root as lleuad) → “Moon’s day” — exactly like English Mon-day.
dydd (day) + Mawrth (Mars) → “Mars’s day” — like French mardi.
dydd (day) + Mercher (Mercury) → “Mercury’s day” — like French mercredi.
dydd (day) + Iau (Jupiter) → “Jupiter’s day” — like French jeudi.
dydd (day) + Gwener (Venus) → “Venus’s day” — like French vendredi.
dydd (day) + Sadwrn (Saturn) → “Saturn’s day” — same logic as English Satur-day.
dydd (day) + Sul (Sun, same root as haul) → “Sun’s day” — same logic as English Sun-day.
Picture pointing right at the ground saying “HETH-yoo — THIS very day”: heddiw = today.
Sounds like “uh-VOR-ee”, close to “before-y” — tomorrow is always just before it arrives: yfory = tomorrow.
Short and sharp, sounds like “though” — “though it’s gone now”: ddoe = yesterday.
wyth (eight) + nos (night) → literally “eight nights” = a week (Welsh counts inclusively from one day to the same day the next week).
pen (head/end) + wythnos (week, just above) → literally “the head/end of the week” = weekend.

title: Colours
blurb: Describe what you see.

items.mnemonic: Sounds like “cock” — picture a red cockerel’s comb: coch = red.
Sounds like “glass” — think of blue sea-glass: glas = blue.
Picture “weird green” — gwyrdd ≈ weird: gwyrdd = green.
Sounds close to “melon” — a yellow melon: melyn = yellow.
Short and sharp, “dee” — dim the lights and you get du (black).
Sounds exactly like “win” — picture a white flag of victory: gwyn = white.
Identical to English “orange” minus the g — oren = orange.
Rhythm close to English “purple” — think “Portaloo, for purple”: porffor = purple.
Identical to English “brown”.
Sounds close to “fluid” — grey like drifting smoke: llwyd = grey.

title: Everyday verbs
blurb: Actions you’ll use all the time.

items.mnemonic: Sounds like “mind” — “mind, I’m going!”: mynd = to go.
Sounds like “dodge” — picture dodging in through the door as you arrive: dod = to come.
Sounds close to “weld” — welding goggles let you see clearly: gweld = to see.
Sounds close to “charade” — charades is a game about talking without talking: siarad = to speak.
Shares its root with bwyd (food, which you’ll see on every menu) — bwyta = to eat.
Sounds close to “up-ed” — “I necked (upped) my drink”: yfed = to drink.
This is the very word in “Dysgu Cymraeg” splashed across this app — you already know dysgu = to learn/teach.
Think of reading a “darn” (piece) of a page — darllen = to read.
Sounds close to “prune-y” — picture pruning your wallet every time you buy something: prynu = to buy.
Sounds like “care-oo” — to love is to care: caru = to love.

title: Useful phrases
blurb: Introduce yourself and get by.

items.mnemonic: fy (my) + enw (name) + i (I, for emphasis) + yw (is) → a logical build-up: “my name, I, is…”.
Dw i’n (I am, the phrase you’ll see constantly) + dysgu (learn — see the verbs lesson) + Cymraeg (Welsh) → “I am learning Welsh”.
Dw i’n (I am) + dod (come — see the verbs lesson) + o (from) → “I am coming from…”.
Dw i (I) + ddim (not — picture a “dim” switch flicked off) + yn deall (understanding) → “I not understanding” = I don’t understand.
Siaradwch (speak! — from siarad, see the verbs lesson) + yn arafach (more slowly) → “speak more slow-er”.
Dw i’n (I am) + hoffi (liking) + coffi (coffee) → the rhyme hoffi/coffi is the memory hook itself: “I’m liking coffee”.
Ble (where) + mae’r (is the) + toiled (toilet, borrowed straight from English) → barely needs translating.
Faint (how much/many) + yw e (is it) → literally “how-much is it”.

items.cy: Ga i de, os gwelwch yn dda?
items.en: Can I have a tea, please?
items.pr: gah ee deh, os GWEL-ooch un thah
items.mnemonic: Ga i (can I have) + de (tea) + os gwelwch yn dda (please — see the greetings lesson) → “get I tea, please”.
Sounds close to “ruin” — “do it now before it’s ruined!” (South Wales says nawr, which sounds just like English “now” — the easier one to remember.)
Wela i (I’ll see — from gweld, see the verbs lesson) + chi (you) + wedyn (after) → “I’ll-see you after” = see you later.

title: Body parts
blurb: Name the parts of your body.

items.mnemonic: Identical to English “pen” — picture a pen balanced on top of your head: pen = head.
Sounds close to “vault” — picture a vault of hair piled on your head: gwallt = hair.
Sounds like “look, gadget” — you need an eye to look at your gadget: llygad = eye.
Sounds close to “true-in” — point it true, right at your nose: trwyn = nose.
Sounds exactly like “keg” — picture a keg (barrel) as one big round mouth: ceg = mouth.
Sounds close to “closed” — cup your hand round your ear to close out noise: clust = ear.
Sounds close to “brake” — pull the brake lever with your arm: braich = arm.
Sounds close to “law” — “raise your hand, that’s the law!”: llaw = hand.
Sounds exactly like “bees” — bees land one at a time on each finger: bys = finger.
Sounds close to “coy” — stand coyly balanced on one leg: coes = leg.
Sounds close to “trod” — “I trod on your foot!”: troed = foot.
Sounds close to “cave-in” — guard your back from a cave-in: cefn = back.
Sounds exactly like “bowl” — a round, bowl-shaped belly: bol = tummy.
Sounds close to “ask with” — shrug your shoulders when you “ask with” a shrug: ysgwydd = shoulder.

title: Rooms and things in the house
blurb: The rooms of the house and what you'll find in them.

items.mnemonic: Shares its root with ceg (mouth, from the body lesson) — the kitchen is the “mouth” of the house, where food goes in.
Sounds like “LOL-va” — picture lolling about on the sofa, laughing “LOL”: lolfa = living room.
ystafell (room) + wely (bed) → literally “room of bed”: bedroom.
ystafell (room) + ymolchi (washing oneself, from golchi “to wash”) → literally “room for washing”: bathroom.
Identical to English “landing” — the floor you land on between stairs.
Identical to English “attic”.
Sounds close to “go-lie” — go lie down: gwely = bed.
Identical to English “sofa”.
Sounds close to “board” — a table is a flat board: bwrdd = table.
Sounds close to “cater” — caterers always set out chairs: cadair = chair.
Sounds close to “furnace” — ffwrn = oven.
Identical to English “sink”, just spelled Welsh-style.
oer (cold) + cell (chamber) → literally “cold chamber”: oergell = fridge.
Identical to English “wardrobe”.
Close to the Latin “fenestra” behind English “fenestration” — ffenestr = window.
Sounds close to “dross” — picture a big D-R-oo-S sign on it: drws = door.
Built the same way as English tele-vision: tele- (far) + a form of gweld/golwg (to see/sight) → “far-seeing” box: teledu = TV.
Sounds almost identical to English “cupboard” itself: cwpwrdd = cupboard.

title: Outside
blurb: The garden, the street and the world beyond your front door.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to English “garden” — in fact the two words share the very same old root: gardd = garden.
Contains coed (trees/woods) — one coeden makes up the coed: coeden = tree.
Think “bloom” — a blodyn blooms: blodyn = flower.
glas (green) + gwellt (grass stalks) → literally “green-grass”: glaswellt = grass.
Sounds close to “aw, air!” — look up and say it: awyr = sky.
Sounds like “howl” — howl at the sun: haul = sun.
Shares its root with Dydd Llun (Monday, “Moon’s day”, from the days lesson): lleuad = moon.
Sounds close to “serene” — a serene, starry night: seren = star.
Identical to English “car”.
Sounds close to “forth” — onward and forth down the road: ffordd = road.
pen (head/end, from the body lesson) + tref (home-town, as in cartref) → literally “head of the home-town” — the settlement at the head of a valley.
The same tref running through cartref (home) and pentref (village) — the core “town/homestead” word.
Sounds close to “mount” with an extra syllable: mynydd = mountain.
Sounds close to “Avon” — the River Avon in England takes its very name from this old Celtic word for river: afon = river.
Sounds exactly like French “mer” (sea) and close to English “more” — the sea has more water than anything: môr = sea.

title: Family relations
blurb: Extended family: aunts, uncles, cousins and in-laws.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “mod rib” — picture your stylish “mod” aunt: modryb = aunt.
Sounds close to “youth-er” — your youthful uncle who still acts young: ewythr = uncle.
Contains cefn (back, from the body lesson) — a handy hook: “the cousin who has your back”: cefnder = male cousin.
Starts with cyf- (co-/shared, as in cyfaill “friend”) and ends like nith (niece) — think “co-niece”: cyfnither = female cousin.
Short and sounds close to English “gore” — remember it as the root behind words like arwr (hero): gŵr = husband.
Simply the female counterpart of gŵr (husband) above — swap the ending and you have “wife”: gwraig.
Sounds close to “mob” — “my mob includes my son”: mab = son (also the root of old Welsh surnames like ap Llywelyn, “son of Llywelyn”).
Sounds close to “merch”-andise — picture a market-seller’s daughter: merch = daughter (also the everyday word for “girl”).
Sounds close to “ewer” (a small jug) — a small jug for a small grandson: ŵyr = grandson.
The female form of ŵyr (grandson) above, with the -es ending you’ll meet again in athrawes (female teacher): wyres = granddaughter.
Sounds close to “nigh” — your nephew is always nigh (near) at family gatherings: nai = nephew.
Sounds almost exactly like English “niece” itself — the closest sound-match on this whole list: nith = niece.

title: Jobs
blurb: Talk about what people do for a living.

items.mnemonic: Shares its root with dysgu (to teach/learn) and gives us athrawes with the -es feminine ending (see wyres, above): athro = teacher.
Sounds very close to English “medic”: meddyg = doctor.
Identical to English “nurse”, just spelled Welsh-style.
fferm (farm, borrowed from English) + -wr (a very common “person who does X” ending, also in gyrrwr, adeiladwr below) → “farm-person”: ffermwr = farmer.
peiriant (machine/engine) + -ydd (another “doer” ending, also in cogydd, pobydd below) → “machine-person”: peiriannydd = engineer.
cog- (cook) + -ydd (the same doer-ending as peiriannydd) → “cook-person”: cogydd = chef.
plis- (police, borrowed from English) + -mon (man) → literally “police-man”, exactly like English: plismon = police officer.
diffodd (put out/extinguish) + -wr (doer-ending) + tân (fire) → literally “put-out-er of fire”: diffoddwr tân = firefighter.
gyrru (to drive) + -wr (the same doer-ending as ffermwr, adeiladwr) → “drive-person”: gyrrwr = driver.
cyfraith (law) + -wr (doer-ending) → “law-person”: cyfreithiwr = lawyer.
pobi (to bake) + -ydd (the same doer-ending as peiriannydd, cogydd) → “bake-person”: pobydd = baker.
adeiladu (to build) + -wr (the same doer-ending as ffermwr, gyrrwr) → “build-person”: adeiladwr = builder.

title: Pronouns
blurb: The words for I, you, he, she, we and they, plus my/your/their.

items.mnemonic: Sounds exactly like English “fee” — picture paying a small fee for yourself: fi = I/me.
Sounds like “tea” — picture offering tea to a close friend (the informal 'you'): ti = you.
Short and sharp — think “veh, him over there”: fe = he/him. (South Wales also uses fo in the north's place.)
Sounds exactly like “he” spelled differently — a useful trap to notice: hi actually means SHE: hi = she/her.
Sounds like “knee” — picture linking knees in a group huddle: ni = we/us.
Sounds like “key” — the key that opens a conversation with a group or a stranger: chi = you (plural/polite).
Short, nasal “noo” — picture a crowd going “noo, noo” in the distance: nhw = they/them.
The vuh in “fy enw i” (my name) from the phrases lesson — fy = my.
Pairs with ti (you, informal) — dy = your, said to a close friend.

items.en: his / her (depends on mutation that follows)
items.mnemonic: Sounds like the letter “A” — a trips you up because it looks the same for 'his' and 'her', only the mutation after it tells you which: ei = his/her.
Sounds like “eye-n” — rhymes with ni (we): ein = our.
Pairs with chi (you, formal/plural) — eich = your, said formally or to a group.
Pairs with nhw (they) — eu = their.
Shows up in words like fy hunan (myself) — hunan = self.

title: Question words
blurb: Who, what, when, where, how, why and which.

items.mnemonic: Sounds like “pooey!” — ask “pooey, who did that?”: pwy = who.
Identical in spelling to the English name “Beth” — picture asking Beth, “what?”: beth = what.
Sounds like “pride” without the final e — “when is the pride parade?”: pryd = when.
You've already met this in “Ble mae'r toiled?” (where is the toilet) — ble = where.
You've already met this in “Sut mae?” (how are you) — sut = how.
Identical to the English name “Pam” — picture asking Pam, “why?”: pam = why.
You've already met this in “Faint yw e?” (how much is it) — faint = how much/many.
Short and sharp, always goes before a noun — “pa liw?” (which colour?): pa = which.

title: Prepositions
blurb: The small linking words: in, on, to, from, with and more.

items.mnemonic: Short and common — the very same yn you'll see inside phrases like “dw i'n” (I am): yn = in.
Identical to the start of English “ar-ea” — picture something sitting ON an area: ar = on.
Just the letter “ee” — the shortest word in the language: i = to.
Just the letter “oh” — “oh, where's that from?”: o = from/of.
Sounds like “gun” — “shot BY someone” — gan always points at the person something comes from: gan = by/from.
Identical to the English word “am” — “what's this am-bout?”: am = for/about.
Identical to the English word “at” — moving AT/towards something: at = towards.
Identical to the name “Dan” — picture Dan hiding under the table: dan = under.
Sounds like “dross” — picture climbing dross (rubbish) piled OVER a wall: dros = over.
Sounds almost like the English word itself — “троу” ≈ “through”: trwy = through.
Sounds like “hub” — a bike with no hub is a wheel heb (without) its centre: heb = without.
This is the rhwng hiding inside rhyngrwyd (internet, “between-net”) — rhwng = between.
Sounds like “kin” — your kin (family) came before you: cyn = before.
ar (on) + ôl (behind/back) → literally “on the back (of)” = after: ar ôl.
Sounds close to “worth” — something worth standing right next to: wrth = by/next to.
Sounds close to “guitar” without the r — strum a guitar WITH a friend: gyda = with.

title: Joining words
blurb: And, or, but, because and the other glue that holds sentences together.

items.mnemonic: Just the letter “a” — the simplest joining word there is: a = and. (Becomes ac before a vowel.)
The a (and) with a hard “c” added so it flows into the next vowel sound — tea ac coffi (tea and coffee): ac = and.
Sounds close to “annoy” without the first bit — “tea neu coffi?” (tea or coffee?): neu = or.
Identical to the end of the English word “bond” — a bond, BUT with conditions: ond = but.
Sounds close to “a chorus” — “I sang because (achos) of the chorus”: achos = because.
Contains achos's cousin — a longer, more formal way to say “because”: oherwydd = because of.
Sounds close to “fell, eh” — “it fell, so (felly) I picked it up”: felly = so.
Sounds close to “heavy, duh” — “that's heavy, also (hefyd) big”: hefyd = also.
Short, sounds like “air” — “despite (er) the thin air, we carried on”: er = although.
Sounds like the start of “tra-ffic” — stuck in traffic WHILE waiting: tra = while.
Identical to the kitchen “pan” — picture a pan boiling over exactly WHEN the timer rings: pan = when.

title: Yes, no and to be
blurb: The small words that answer questions and the core forms of “to be”.

items.mnemonic: The “I am” form used to answer a question that starts with ydw/ydy — ydw = I am.
Pairs with ti (you) — wyt = you are.
The most useful little word in the language — ydy = is.
The plural cousin of ydy — ydyn = are (we/they).
Pairs with chi (you, formal) — ydych = are (you).
Sounds exactly like “mine” — “mine, they are!”: maen = are (they).
Sounds close to “oyster” without the -ter — “is there an oyster in this?”: oes = is/are there.
Simply nac (not) + oes (is there) → the “no” answer to oes: nac oes.
Short, sounds like “yeah” said quickly — ie = yes.
Sounds close to “nah, gay” — just hear the “nah”: nage = no.

title: Common adjectives
blurb: Big, small, good, bad, and all the describing words in between.

items.mnemonic: Sounds exactly like English “more” — more of something makes it mawr (big).
Sounds close to “bark” — even a small dog has a big bach (bark)! bach = small.
You've already met this everywhere — bore da, nos da — da = good.
Sounds close to “drug” — bad things, drwg, are often linked to drugs: drwg = bad.
Sounds almost identical to English “happy-ish” — hapus = happy.
Nearly identical to English “triste” (French for sad) — trist = sad.
Sounds close to “poached” — a poached egg is served poeth (hot): poeth = hot.
Sounds close to “oyer”, close to “ower” in “shower” — a cold shower: oer = cold.
Identical to English “hen” — picture an old hen that's been around for years: hen = old.
Sounds close to “new width” — a newydd (new) road has a new width: newydd = new.
Sounds close to “how, though” — “how, though — that was hawdd (easy)!”: hawdd = easy.
Starts with an- like English negative prefixes (annoy, etc.) — the opposite of hawdd (easy): anodd = difficult.
Sounds close to “cuff 'em quick” — too cyflym (fast) to catch: cyflym = fast.
Sounds close to “a raft” — a raft drifts araf (slowly) downstream: araf = slow.
Sounds close to “pressure” — busy people are under pressure: prysur = busy.
Sounds exactly like English “towel” — a towel muffles sound, keeping things tawel (quiet): tawel = quiet.
Sounds close to “clan” — a clean, tidy clan's house: glân = clean.
Sounds close to “bidder” — the dirtiest bidder at the auction: budr = dirty.
Sounds close to “grief” — strong enough to carry your grief: cryf = strong.
Sounds exactly like “gone” — weak energy, all gone: gwan = weak.
Nearly identical to English “pert” — pert = pretty (common in the south; North Wales often says tlws instead).
Nearly identical to English “tall” — tal = tall.
Sounds exactly like “beer” — a short glass of beer: byr = short.
Sounds close to “tomb” — a heavy stone tomb: trwm = heavy.
Sounds close to “ask a van” — light enough to not need a van: ysgafn = light.
Sounds close to “rad”, as in “that's rad (and cheap)!”: rhad = cheap.
Sounds close to “dread” — the price you dread: drud = expensive.
Shares its root with agor (to open, from the verbs lesson) — agored = open.
Shares its root with cau (to close, from the verbs lesson) — caeedig = closed.
Sounds close to “gag” — an empty stomach makes you gag: gwag = empty.
Sounds close to “lawn” — a lawn full of grass: llawn = full.

title: More everyday verbs
blurb: The verbs you'll reach for constantly: to be, to have, to do, to want.

items.en: to be / that (reporting what someone said or thinks)
items.mnemonic: The single most important verb in the language — every "dw i" (I am) comes from bod. It also means "that" when reporting speech: dw i'n meddwl bod... (I think that...).

items.en: to have / to get / to be allowed
items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “kyle” — Kyle always gets to have the best toys: cael = to have/get.
Sounds close to “good made” — if you made it well, you gwneud (did) it right: gwneud = to do/make.
Sounds close to “gallery” — you need to be able to reach the top shelf of the gallery: gallu = can.
Sounds close to “gore-vod” — you simply must deal with gore in a horror film: gorfod = must.
Sounds close to “age, ah” — “ah, I want to be that age again”: eisiau = to want. (South Wales often says moyn.)
Sounds close to “a rose” — wait for a rose to bloom: aros = to wait.
Sounds close to “Edric” — picture Edric always looking around: edrych = to look.
Sounds close to “grand, oh” — “oh, how grand, I'm listening!”: gwrando = to listen.
Shares its root with meddyg (doctor, from the jobs lesson) — doctors think hard: meddwl = to think.
Sounds close to “cough, yo” — “yo, remember to cover that cough!”: cofio = to remember.
Starts with an- (not) + cofio (remember) → literally “not-remember”: anghofio = to forget.
Sounds close to “cody” — Cody always gets up early: codi = to get up.
Sounds close to “iced, the-” — sit down for some iced tea: eistedd = to sit.
Sounds close to “sever ill” — stand firm even when you sever something: sefyll = to stand.
Sounds close to “red-egg” — run fast carrying a red egg: rhedeg = to run.
Sounds close to “curded” — a slow, curdled walk: cerdded = to walk.
Shares its root with gyrrwr (driver, from the jobs lesson) — gyrru = to drive.
Sounds close to “a gore” — open the gate carefully: agor = to open.
Sounds close to “kye”, close to “sky” without the s — close the window before the sky clouds over: cau = to close.
Sounds close to “Roy” — Roy always gives generously: rhoi = to give.
Shares its root with the question word pattern — gofyn = to ask.
Sounds close to “at web” — answer the question posted at the web link: ateb = to answer.
Sounds close to “quarry, eye” — children play (chwarae) by the quarry: chwarae = to play.
Shares its root with gwaith (work/occasion, from the greetings lesson's noswaith) — gweithio = to work.
Sounds close to “byoo-tiful” (beautiful) — it's beautiful to byw (live) well: byw = to live.
Sounds close to “marrow” — even bone marrow eventually marw (dies): marw = to die.
Sounds close to “wertha-in” — burst out laughing at the werther-ing: chwerthin = to laugh.
Sounds almost identical to English “cry, oh” — crio = to cry.
Sounds close to “cannot be” sung badly — practice until you can sing: canu = to sing.

title: Bigger numbers
blurb: Eleven, twenty, a hundred, a thousand — and how Welsh builds them.

items.mnemonic: un (one) + deg (ten) + un (one) → literally “one-ten-one” = 10+1 = 11. (You'll also hear the older un ar ddeg, “one on ten”.)
The classic word for twelve, still used constantly for telling time (“deuddeg o'r gloch” = 12 o'clock): deuddeg = twelve.
pump (five) + deg (ten) fused together → “five-ten” = 15: pymtheg = fifteen.
The classic, still-dominant word for 20 in everyday speech (modern decimal dau ddeg also works): ugain = twenty.
tri (three) + deg (ten) → “three-ten(s)” = 30: tri deg = thirty.
pedwar (four) + deg (ten) → “four-ten(s)” = 40: pedwar deg = forty.
pump (five, shortened to pum before a noun) + deg (ten) → “five-ten(s)” = 50: pum deg = fifty.
Sounds exactly like English “cant” — a hundred percent, not a cant (lean): cant = a hundred.
Sounds exactly like English “meal” — a thousand meals: mil = a thousand.

title: Time words
blurb: Minutes, hours, months, years — and words like always, sometimes and never.

items.mnemonic: Nearly identical to English “minute”: munud.
Sounds exactly like English “our” — our hour: awr = hour.
Contains dydd-like echoes of “day” — diwrnod = a whole day, as opposed to dydd used in weekday names.
Sounds exactly like English “mees”, close to “meese” — a month of geese: mis = month.
Contains blwydd, the same root as pen-blwydd (birthday, “head of year”): blwyddyn = year.
canol (middle) + dydd (day) → literally “middle of the day” = noon: canol dydd.
canol (middle) + nos (night) → literally “middle of the night” = midnight: canol nos.
Shares its root with gwaith (occasion/time) — weithiau = sometimes, some occasions.
bob (every) + amser (time) → literally “every time” = always: bob amser.
Sounds close to “bith-er”, close to “bitter” — never going back to that bitter taste: byth = never.
Sounds close to “gunner” — the early-bird gunner: yn gynnar = early.
Sounds close to “hoo-ear” — you only hear the clock strike once you're already late: yn hwyr = late.

title: Months
blurb: The twelve months of the year.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “your honour” — a new year begins with “your honour, Ionawr (January)”: Ionawr = January.
Sounds close to “chivalry” mangled — short month, short word: Chwefror = February.
The same word as Dydd Mawrth (Tuesday) and the planet Mars — Mawrth = March.
Nearly identical to English “April” rearranged — Ebrill = April.
Identical to English “my” and almost identical to “May” itself: Mai = May.
Sounds close to “the heaven” — June, the month that feels like heaven: Mehefin = June.
Contains gorffen (to finish) — the first half of summer finishing: Gorffennaf = July.
Nearly identical to English “August” shortened: Awst = August.
Sounds close to “medi(um)” — the medium month, the harvest month: Medi = September. (Medi is also the verb “to harvest”.)
The very same word as hydref (autumn, the season) — October IS the autumn month: Hydref = October.
Sounds close to “tacked, weathered” — November's tacked-on weather: Tachwedd = November.
Contains rhag (before/against) — the month before (rhag) the new year: Rhagfyr = December.

title: Seasons
blurb: Spring, summer, autumn and winter.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “gone, win” — winter's gone, spring's won: gwanwyn = spring.
Sounds exactly like English “have” — you always have a summer holiday: haf = summer.
The very same word as the month Hydref (October) — autumn's signature month: hydref = autumn.
Sounds close to “gave off” — winter gives off a chill: gaeaf = winter.

title: Weather
blurb: Talk about rain, sun, wind and everything in between.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “tooth, width” — weather changes with the width of the season: tywydd = weather.
Sounds exactly like English “glow” — rain makes puddles glow under streetlights: glaw = rain.
Sounds close to “Ayra” — pictures a snow-white name: eira = snow.
Sounds close to “gwynt” ≈ “wint(er)” — the winter wind: gwynt = wind.
haul (sun, from the outside lesson) + -og (adjective ending, “full of”) → “full of sun”: heulog = sunny.
cwmwl (cloud) + -og (full of) → “full of cloud”: cymylog = cloudy.
storm + -us (adjective ending) → “full of storm”: stormus = stormy.
Sounds close to “newel” (a staircase post) — fog so thick you can't see the newel post: niwl = fog.
Sounds close to “rev” — a car engine that won't rev in the frost: rhew = ice/frost.
Shares its root with tymhorau (seasons) — both come from the same “time/season” root: tymheredd = temperature.

title: Shopping and money
blurb: Prices, pounds, pence and the till.

items.mnemonic: Nearly identical to English “shop”: siop = shop.
Sounds close to “Aryan” rearranged — think “a rain of money”: arian = money. (Arian also means “silver”.)
Sounds exactly like English “punt” — a financial punt (bet) worth a punt (pound): punt = pound.
Sounds close to “cane, yoga” — bend like yoga to pick up a penny: ceiniog = penny.
Sounds close to “worth you” — “it's worth you selling that”: gwerthu = to sell.
Nearly identical to English “price”: pris = price.
Nearly identical to English “bill”: bil = bill.
Contains derbyn (to receive) — a receipt is proof you derbyn (received) something: derbynneb = receipt.
Nearly identical to English “cardin(al)” shortened — cerdyn = card.
Sounds close to “march, nod” — march to the market and nod at the stalls: marchnad = market.

title: Travel and transport
blurb: Trains, buses, planes and the words you'll need at the airport.

items.mnemonic: Nearly identical to English “train”: trên = train.
Nearly identical to English “bus”: bws = bus.
Shares its root with awyr (sky, from the outside lesson) — an awyren flies through the awyr: awyren = aeroplane.
Sounds close to “long” — a long ship: llong = ship.
maes (field) + awyr (sky/air) → literally “field of air” = airport: maes awyr.
Sounds close to “gore's half” — half the gore ends at the station: gorsaf = station.
Sounds close to “token” — a ticket is just another token: tocyn = ticket.
Nearly identical to English “passport”: pasport = passport.
Sounds close to “goo, I lie” — lie on the beach during the holidays: gwyliau = holidays.
Sounds close to “tithe” — a journey you pay a toll (tithe) for: taith = journey.
Identical to English “map”: map = map.
Nearly identical to English “bike”: beic = bike.

title: Clothes
blurb: What you're wearing, from head to toe.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “the lad's” — the lad's clothes: dillad = clothes.
Sounds close to “crease” — a shirt always creases: crys = shirt.
Nearly identical to English “trousers”: trowsus = trousers.
Nearly identical to English “frock”: ffrog = dress.
Sounds close to “as kid, yeah” — as a kid, yeah, you need shoes: esgidiau = shoes.
Nearly identical to English “coat”: cot = coat.
Nearly identical to English “hat”: het = hat.
Sounds close to “men, egg” — men handling eggs wear gloves: menig = gloves.
Nearly identical to English “scarf”: sgarff = scarf.
Sounds close to “sand eye” — sandy socks after the beach: sanau = socks.

title: School
blurb: Classrooms, books and lessons.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “ask all” — ask all your questions at school: ysgol = school.
Contains myfyrio (to study/reflect) + -wr (the “person who does X” ending from the jobs lesson): myfyriwr = student.
prif (chief/main) + ysgol (school) → literally “main school” = university: prifysgol.
Sounds close to “liver” — a book as thick as a liver: llyfr = book.
Nearly identical to English “pencil”: pensil = pencil.
Nearly identical to English “paper”: papur = paper.
Sounds close to “our hollow odd” — exams leave you feeling hollow: arholiad = exam.
Sounds close to “verse” — learn a new verse every lesson: gwers = lesson.
gwaith (work) + cartref (home, from the family lesson) → literally “home work”: gwaith cartref = homework.
Sounds close to “dose, Bart” — Bart gets his daily dose of class: dosbarth = classroom.

title: Animals
blurb: Pets and farmyard favourites.

items.mnemonic: Sounds almost exactly like English “an-i-vile”, close to “animal” itself: anifail = animal.
Sounds exactly like “key” — a dog guards the key: ci = dog. (This is the very cath/ci pairing used in the mutations lesson!)
This is the exact word used throughout the mutations lesson (cath, dy gath, fy nghath, ei chath) — cath = cat.
Sounds close to “kev-ill” — Kevin's ill horse: ceffyl = horse.
Sounds close to “davit, add” — add a sheep to the flock: dafad = sheep.
Sounds close to “mock in” — mock the pig as it rolls in mud: mochyn = pig.
Sounds exactly like “yarr!” (pirate noise) — a hen clucking “yarr”: iâr = hen.
Sounds close to “a deryn” — picture “a derring” little bird: aderyn = bird.
Sounds close to “piss, god, in” — a fish swims straight in: pysgodyn = fish.
Sounds close to “look, oh, den” — a mouse looks for its den: llygoden = mouse.

title: Technology
blurb: Computers, phones and the internet.

items.mnemonic: cyfrif (to count/calculate) + -iadur (device ending) → literally “counting-device”: cyfrifiadur = computer.
Nearly identical to English “phone”: ffôn = phone.
rhwng (between, from the prepositions lesson) + rhwyd (net) → literally “between-net” = internet: rhyngrwyd.
e- (electronic, same as English) + post (mail) → exactly parallel to English “e-mail”: e-bost = email.
gwe (web) + man (place) → literally “web-place” = website: gwefan.
Contains cymhwyso (to apply/qualify) — the thing you apply/use: cymhwysiad = app.
cyfrin (secret) + gair (word) → literally “secret-word” = password: cyfrinair.
Nearly identical to English “screen”: sgrin = screen.

title: Feelings
blurb: How you're feeling, beyond just happy or sad.

items.mnemonic: Shares its root with caru (to love, from the verbs lesson) — cariad = love/sweetheart.
Sounds close to “oven” — fear of a hot oven: ofn = fear.
Short and sharp, sounds like “dig” — dig in when you're angry: dig = angry.
Sounds close to “sun dodge” — dodge the sun in surprise: syndod = surprise.
Sounds close to “balk” — too proud to balk at anything: balch = proud.
blino (to tire) + -edig (adjective ending) → “tired out”: blinedig = tired.
newyn (hunger/famine) + -og (full of) → “full of hunger”: newynog = hungry.
syched (thirst, related to sych “dry”) + -edig → “made dry/thirsty”: sychedig = thirsty.
Shares its root with un (one, from the numbers lesson) — alone, like the number one: unig = lonely.
cyffro (excitement/stir) + -us (full of) → “full of excitement”: cyffrous = excited.

title: Directions and position
blurb: Left, right, up, down, near and far.

items.mnemonic: Sounds close to “quith”, close to “with” — turn with your left hand: chwith = left.
Short, sounds like “deh” — the same word covers both “right” (direction) and “south” (as in De Cymru, South Wales): de.
i (to) + fyny (up, related to the word for “above”) → literally “to up”: i fyny = up.
i (to) + lawr (down) → literally “to down”: i lawr = down.
Sounds close to “you, ma” — “you, ma, come here!”: yma = here.
Rhymes with yma (here) — its opposite number: yna = there.
Sounds close to “a goss(ip)” — gossip spreads fastest among people standing near each other: agos = near.
Sounds close to “pell(et)” — a pellet fired far away: pell = far.
Shares its root with canol dydd (midday) and canol nos (midnight) from the time lesson — canol = middle.
Nearly identical to English “cornel”, close to “corner”: cornel = corner.

title: Everyday objects
blurb: Cups, plates, keys and the small things you handle all day.

items.mnemonic: Nearly identical to English “cup, an”: cwpan = cup.
Nearly identical to English “plate”: plât = plate.
Sounds close to “cull, hell” — a knife you'd want to cull from the kitchen: cyllell = knife.
Nearly identical to English “fork”: fforc = fork.
Sounds close to “Louie” — Louie always loses his spoon: llwy = spoon.
Nearly identical to English “bottle”: potel = bottle.
Nearly identical to English “box”: bocs = box.
Sounds close to “all, weth(er)” — whatever the weather, you need your key: allwedd = key.
Identical to English “bag”: bag = bag.
Nearly identical to English “umbrella” rearranged: ymbarél = umbrella.

title: Celebrations and farewells
blurb: Birthdays, Christmas and the formal way to say goodbye.

items.mnemonic: A long word for a big moment — just remember it starts like “long” and means a big “congratulations”: Llongyfarchiadau.
pen (head/end, from the body lesson) + blwydd (year, from blwyddyn) + hapus (happy) → literally “happy head-of-year”, exactly like pen-wythnos (weekend): Pen-blwydd hapus.
Nadolig (Christmas) + llawen (merry/joyful) → Nadolig Llawen = Merry Christmas.
blwyddyn (year) + newydd (new) + dda (good) → literally “good new year”: Blwyddyn Newydd Dda.
croeso (welcome, from the greetings lesson) + i (to) + Gymru (Wales, mutated from Cymru) → Croeso i Gymru.
da (good) + boch (may it be) + chi (you, formal) → a formal farewell, literally “may it be well with you”: Da boch chi.

title: Handy connectors and fillers
blurb: The little words that make you sound like a fluent speaker.

items.mnemonic: wrth (by) + gwrs (course) → a direct echo of English “of course”: wrth gwrs.
Sounds close to “a valley, eye” — maybe there's a valley, maybe not: efallai = maybe.
siŵr (sure) + o fod (of being) → literally “sure to be”: siŵr o fod = must be.
Contains pendant (decisive/definite) — yn bendant = definitely.
mewn (in) + gwirionedd (truth, from gwir “true”) → literally “in truth”: mewn gwirionedd = actually.
a (and) + dweud (to say) + y gwir (the truth) → literally “and to say the truth”: a dweud y gwir.
dim (not/no, from the phrases lesson's ddim) + problem (direct borrowing) → dim problem = no problem.
popeth (everything) + yn iawn (okay/right) → literally “everything okay”: popeth yn iawn.
